title: Which Family Court in Delhi Can Hear Your Divorce, Maintenance or Custody Case
meta_description: Which Delhi family court complex has jurisdiction over your divorce, maintenance or custody case, decided by residence, not convenience.
intro: A divorce, maintenance or custody petition in Delhi cannot be filed at whichever family court is nearest or most convenient. The Family Courts Act, 1984 gives a family court exclusive jurisdiction over the matters that fall within its own territorial limits, and those limits are fixed by notification, not by where either spouse happens to find a lawyer. Filing in the wrong court usually does not end the case outright, but it invites an early objection on jurisdiction that can cost months before the real dispute is even reached.

This guide sets out how Delhi's family courts are organised by district, how the residence test under the Hindu Marriage Act decides which district actually applies to a given couple, and what options exist if a case ends up filed in the wrong place or a party genuinely cannot litigate where the other side wants to fight it. Our guides on How Indian Courts Decide Child Custody and Mediation in Matrimonial Disputes cover what happens once a case is properly before the right court.

sections.heading: Family courts have exclusive jurisdiction within their own area
paragraphs: The Family Courts Act, 1984 was enacted to set up specialised courts for matrimonial and related family disputes, and once a family court is established for an area, it takes over the jurisdiction that an ordinary district or civil court would otherwise have exercised there. A family court's power is not optional or concurrent with the district court for matters the Act covers; a petition that falls within a given family court's territorial area has to be filed there, and that court alone can try it.

Delhi has several family court complexes, each covering a defined set of districts of the National Capital Territory, and new complexes and realignments have been added over the years as the city's district structure has itself changed. Because of this, the correct complex for a given address is not always the one closest to where a couple actually lived, and the current list of districts assigned to each complex should be confirmed with the Delhi District Courts before a petition is drafted, rather than assumed from an older article or a previous case.

sections.heading: The complexes and the districts they generally cover
paragraphs: Delhi's family courts sit at several complexes, including Patiala House, Dwarka, Rohini, Saket and Karkardooma, each handling matrimonial and family matters for a cluster of the city's judicial districts. Patiala House's family court was set up to take family matters arising in the New Delhi district, Dwarka's complex serves the South-West district, Rohini generally covers the North-West and Outer districts, Karkardooma covers the East, North-East and Shahdara districts, and Saket covers the South-East district, broadly matching how Delhi's district courts themselves are organised.

This allocation is set by official notification and has shifted as Delhi added new judicial districts over the years, so a petition drafted on the basis of a years-old list risks being filed at the wrong complex even where the underlying residence facts have not changed at all. The safer practice is to check the current assignment for the specific locality against the Delhi District Courts website or a recent High Court notice before filing, and to flag the point explicitly with the court if there is any doubt about which complex the address actually falls under.

sections.heading: What decides which district applies to your case
paragraphs: Jurisdiction in a Hindu Marriage Act matter follows Section 19 of that Act, which lists the places where a petition can be filed: where the marriage was solemnised, where the respondent resides at the time the petition is filed, where the parties last resided together, or, if the petitioner is the wife, where she is residing on the date the petition is presented. That wife's-residence ground was added by a 2003 amendment and is now one of the most commonly relied on grounds in practice, since it lets a wife file close to wherever she is currently living rather than being tied to the matrimonial home or her husband's address.

Once Section 19 identifies which place has jurisdiction, and that place falls within a Delhi family court's territorial area, that court gets exclusive jurisdiction over the case under the Act. A petitioner who lists an address that does not genuinely satisfy any of the Section 19 grounds, for instance a relative's flat visited only occasionally, is taking on an avoidable risk, because the other side can raise the point as a preliminary objection and force an early hearing purely on where the case belongs rather than on the merits.

Couples who moved out of Delhi into Noida, Gurugram or another part of the National Capital Region before separating sometimes assume the Delhi courts remain available simply because the marriage was solemnised there years earlier, or because one spouse's family still lives in the city. That ground does exist under Section 19, but it sits alongside the respondent's residence and the last shared residence as separate, independent grounds, and a petitioner cannot pick whichever one happens to suit a preferred court if the facts underlying that ground are not genuinely true.

sections.heading: Maintenance applications can follow a different track
paragraphs: A maintenance claim does not have to go through the family court at all. Since 1 July 2024, an application for maintenance of a wife, children or parents is filed under Section 144 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, which replaced Section 125 of the old Code of Criminal Procedure and carries forward substantially the same scheme before a Magistrate, while a petition already pending under the old Section 125 before that date continues under it. A maintenance claim connected to a pending matrimonial petition, by contrast, is more commonly pressed as an interim application within the family court case itself, so which route applies in a given matter depends on whether a matrimonial case is already on file and where.

Choosing the Magistrate's route or the family court route is not purely a matter of preference, since each carries its own procedure and timeline, and a petitioner juggling both a matrimonial case and a separate maintenance application should take care that the two are not pulling in different directions, for example by seeking inconsistent interim relief in each.

sections.heading: Transferring a case once it is filed
paragraphs: Section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure lets a party apply to transfer a pending suit, appeal or proceeding, including a matrimonial case, from one court to another where the ends of justice require it. The Supreme Court has repeatedly held, including in its 2022 decision in N.C.V. Aishwarya v. A.S. Saravana Karthik Sha, that a wife's convenience and difficulty in litigating away from where she lives is generally given real weight when deciding such a transfer petition, though the test remains whether justice genuinely requires the move rather than simple inconvenience to either side.

A transfer petition is not a substitute for filing correctly in the first place, and courts expect a party to have made a genuine attempt to identify the right forum under Section 19 before asking for a transfer on convenience grounds. It is also not available as a routine tool to delay proceedings, and an application made late, or repeated after an earlier one has failed, draws scepticism from the court hearing it.

sections.heading: Common mistakes that invite a jurisdiction fight
paragraphs: Filing at the complex nearest to a lawyer's office rather than the one that actually covers the relevant address is a surprisingly frequent error, particularly where a couple's matrimonial home sat near the border between two districts. Listing a temporary or borrowed address purely to establish residence in a preferred district is another, and it tends to unravel quickly once the other side's lawyer asks pointed questions about how long the petitioner has actually lived there and produces utility bills or neighbours' statements that say otherwise.

A less obvious mistake is assuming that because an earlier proceeding, a protection order or a domestic incident report, was filed in one district, every later matrimonial petition must follow it there automatically. Each application is assessed on its own facts under Section 19, and consistency with an earlier filing helps only if the underlying residence facts genuinely support it. Parties sometimes also skip the step of checking whether a family court even exists yet for a newly carved judicial district, and end up filing before the ordinary district court by mistake, a defect that is usually curable but adds delay that a short search beforehand would have avoided.

faqs.q: How do I find out which family court complex covers my address in Delhi?
faqs.a: Check the current district-to-complex assignment on the Delhi District Courts website or a recent Delhi High Court notice, since the list has changed over the years as new judicial districts were created. Do not rely on an older article, including this one, without confirming the current position for your specific locality.

faqs.q: Can my wife file for divorce in Delhi even though we got married elsewhere and I now live in another city?
faqs.a: Yes, generally. Section 19 of the Hindu Marriage Act lets the wife file where she is residing on the date she presents the petition, a ground added by a 2003 amendment, independent of where the marriage was solemnised or where the husband now lives.

faqs.q: Can I get a maintenance case transferred the same way as a divorce case?
faqs.a: Maintenance proceedings follow their own forum and procedure, and a transfer application in a connected matrimonial case does not automatically carry a separate maintenance proceeding along with it. Each needs to be addressed on its own terms, including under Section 24 of the Civil Procedure Code where it applies.

faqs.q: Will the court transfer my case to Delhi just because it is more convenient for me?
faqs.a: Convenience helps but is not decisive on its own. Courts, including the Supreme Court in its 2022 ruling, give real weight to a wife's difficulty in litigating away from home, but the underlying test remains whether the ends of justice require the transfer, not mere preference.

faqs.q: Does every Delhi family court case go through mediation first?
faqs.a: Matrimonial and family disputes are routinely referred to mediation at the outset in Delhi's family courts, though referral is for the court to decide on the facts of the case rather than being automatic in every matter. Our guide on mediation in matrimonial disputes covers what that process involves.

verification_notes: Family courts having exclusive jurisdiction within their own territorial area under the Family Courts Act, 1984: confirmed from two independent commentary sources describing the same statutory scheme in materially consistent terms.

Delhi's family court complexes at Patiala House, Dwarka, Rohini, Saket and Karkardooma, and their district coverage: confirmed across a 2012 news report on the Patiala House complex opening, a Delhi High Court public notice naming the Dwarka and other principal judges, and a legal guide listing district coverage; the guide flags that this allocation changes over time and should be confirmed currently, since the sources themselves were of different dates.

Hindu Marriage Act Section 19 grounds, including the wife's-residence clause added in 2003: confirmed from a case summary of the amendment and separate commentary describing the same clause in consistent terms.

BNSS Section 144 replacing CrPC Section 125 from 1 July 2024, with pending Section 125 petitions continuing under the old provision: confirmed from two independent legal commentary sources describing the same transition and effective date; a disagreement between sources on whether the word 'minor' was omitted with substantive effect is noted as unresolved and not stated as settled.

N.C.V. Aishwarya v. A.S. Saravana Karthik Sha (2022) and the general principle on wife's convenience in Section 24 transfer petitions: confirmed from two independent reports of the same Supreme Court ruling.
